keyVerseText: And he arose and went: and, behold, a man of Ethiopia, an eunuch of great authority under Candace queen of the Ethiopians, who had the charge of all her treasure, and had come to Jerusalem for to worship,
rootMeaning: The term Κανδάκη (Kandákē) is of foreign origin and does not have a Greek root word, indicating it is a proper name rather than a descriptive term. It specifically refers to an Egyptian queen, Candace, a title for a queen or queen mother in ancient Ethiopia. This literal sense as a regal title adds a layer of historical and cultural specificity beyond the common English gloss, highlighting the prominence and authority associated with the name.
usageInScripture: This word appears only once in Scripture, in Acts 8:27, where it is translated as 'under Candace,' referring to the Ethiopian queen's authority. The consistent use of the term as a proper noun for a queen reveals its function as a title denoting royal status and governance. Its singular occurrence underscores its unique identification of a historical figure rather than a general concept.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding Κανδάκη as a title for an Ethiopian queen enriches our comprehension of the global reach of the Gospel, demonstrating that God's plan includes diverse peoples and rulers. The mention of a high-ranking official 'under Candace' in Scripture emphasizes the sovereignty of God over all earthly authorities and the inclusivity of the Christian faith. Recognizing this term's cultural and political weight helps believers appreciate the historical reality that the Gospel transcended ethnic and national boundaries, fulfilling Jesus' commission to all nations.
keyVerseReflection: Acts 8:27 describes a man of Ethiopia who is an eunuch of great authority 'under Candace queen of the Ethiopians.' The use of Κανδάκη here identifies the political structure and the source of the eunuch's authority, grounding the narrative in a real historical context. This detail highlights the significance of the Ethiopian official's faith journey, showing that even those serving in high positions under foreign monarchs are part of God's redemptive plan.
